pages.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths
pages.content:
When you create a link, you're giving the browser directions to a new destination. Just like with real-world directions, you can give a full, complete address or a simpler, partial one. This is the difference between an **absolute path** and a **relative path**.

---

Let's use a simple analogy: giving a friend directions.

**Absolute Path (The Full Address):**

- Imagine telling your friend, "Go to **1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA**." This is a complete address. No matter where your friend is starting from, they can find that exact location.
- In HTML, an **absolute path** is a link to another website. It always includes the full URL, starting with `https://` or `http://`.

**Example:** `Google`

---

**Relative Path (The Local Directions):**

- Imagine telling your friend, "Go to the **coffee shop next door**." This is a partial address. It only works if your friend is starting from your current location.
- In HTML, a **relative path** is a link to another file *within your own website*. The path is relative to the location of the current file.

**Example:** `About Us`

The browser will look for a file named `about.html` in the **same folder** as the page you are currently on.

pages.title: Anchor Links - Navigating within the Same Page
pages.content:
So far, you've learned to create links that take you to new pages. But what if you have a very long page and want to create a "Table of Contents" that jumps to different sections?


- That's where **anchor links** come in. An anchor link allows you to navigate to a specific spot on the **same page**, without a page reload.
- Think of it like a table of contents in a book. You don't have to turn to a new book; you just jump to a new section within the same book.

---
To make an anchor link work, you need two key parts:
1. **The Destination:** You must give the element you want to jump to a unique name using the `id` attribute.
 * `id` stands for "identifier."
 * **Example:** `Section 1`
2. **The Link:** You create a regular anchor tag, but the `href` attribute starts with a `#` symbol, followed by the name of the destination `id`.
 * **Example:** `Go to Section 1`

The `#` symbol is the key. It tells the browser, "Don't go to a new page. Instead, look for an element with this `id` on the page you're currently viewing."

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Anchor Links - Navigating within the Same Page demonstrates a core HTML concept. Use valid structure, semantic elements, and accessible attributes where applicable.

pages.title: Image Tag Attributes
pages.content: The `` tag is what you use to put pictures on your webpage. It doesn't have a closing tag. Instead, all the information it needs is placed inside the tag itself using attributes. --- - **`src` (Source)** : This is the most important part. The `src` attribute tells the browser where to find the image file. It's the path or web address of your picture.\ **Example:** `` - **`alt` (Alternative Text)**: This provides a simple text description of the image. The `alt` text is very important for two reasons: 1. **Accessibility:** Screen readers will read this text to people who can't see the image. 2. **Fallback:** If the image can't be loaded, the browser will show this text instead.\ **Example:** `` - **`width` and `height`**: These attributes set the size of your image in pixels. Including them helps your page load smoothly. It reserves the correct space for the image, so other content doesn't move around while the picture is loading. **Example:** ``

pages.title: The video Tag with controls
pages.content:
### Video

Use `<video controls>` to embed playable video. A nested `<source>` can specify the media file and its MIME type. Include fallback text for unsupported playback.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: The video Tag with controls demonstrates a core HTML concept. Use valid structure, semantic elements, and accessible attributes where applicable.

codeCard.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>The video Tag with controls</title>
</head>
<body>
  <video controls width="640"><source src="media/lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">Your browser does not support video.</video>
</body>
</html>
